title: Ἥρης δόλος
titleEn: Hera’s Plan and Aphrodite’s Strap — Iliad 14.109–221
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Diomedes, the youngest of the wounded kings, answers Agamemnon’s call for a plan. He recalls his father Tydeus and the family from Aetolia, and proposes that the kings go to the fighting though wounded, keep out of range of the missiles, and push on the men who are holding back. Poseidon, disguised as an old man, takes Agamemnon’s hand and says the gods are not yet wholly against Agamemnon; then he shouts so loudly that every Achaean’s heart is filled with strength. On Olympus Hera sees him at work and sees Zeus sitting on Ida, and she decides to cheat Zeus by making herself desirable. She goes to her chamber, cleanses and anoints herself and dresses, then calls Aphrodite apart and asks for love and longing, saying she is going to settle a quarrel between Oceanus and Tethys. Aphrodite agrees and gives her the embroidered strap that holds every charm.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ καὶ μετέειπε βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Διομήδης·
sentences.tr: toisi de kai meteeipe boēn agathos Diomēdēs·
sentences.l: And among them spoke also Diomedes, good at the war-cry:
sentences.i: And Diomedes, good at the war-cry, also spoke among them:
sentences.n: Agamemnon has just asked for a better plan, and Diomedes answers. τοῖσι is the epic dative plural of the pronoun-article, ‘among them’, and μετέειπε is μετά + ἔειπε, ‘spoke among’. βοὴν ἀγαθός ‘good at the war-cry’ is Diomedes’ stock epithet (βοήν is an accusative of respect), translated every time in the same way. He is about to say that he is the youngest of those present.

sentences.t: ἐγγὺς ἀνήρ·
sentences.tr: engys anēr·
sentences.l: “Near is a man;
sentences.i: “A man is near at hand;
sentences.n: ἐγγὺς ἀνήρ has no verb, ‘near (is) a man’, and ἀνήρ has no article: the man is not named, and Diomedes goes on to speak of the counsel he himself can give. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line, and the speech has no quotation marks in the Greek.

sentences.t: οὐ δηθὰ ματεύσομεν·
sentences.tr: ou dētha mateusomen·
sentences.l: not for long shall we seek;
sentences.i: we shall not be searching for long;
sentences.n: οὐ δηθά is ‘not for long’ (δηθά is an adverb), and ματεύσομεν is the future of ματεύω ‘search, seek’, first person plural. The unit begins mid-line, after the ano teleia, and ends at the next one.

sentences.t:
αἴ κ’ ἐθέλητε
πείθεσθαι, καὶ μή τι κότῳ ἀγάσησθε ἕκαστος
οὕνεκα δὴ γενεῆφι νεώτατός εἰμι μεθ’ ὑμῖν·
sentences.tr:
ai k’ ethelēte
peithesthai, kai mē ti kotōi agasēsthe hekastos
houneka dē geneēphi neōtatos eimi meth’ hymin·
sentences.i: if you are willing to obey, and none of you is indignant in resentment because I am the youngest among you in birth;
sentences.n: αἴ κ’ ἐθέλητε is ‘if you are willing’: αἰ is the dialect form of εἰ, and κε (= ἄν) goes with the subjunctive. μή τι … ἀγάσησθε is a second condition under the same αἴ κε (μή with the aorist subjunctive of ἀγάομαι ‘be indignant’, joined to ἐθέλητε), ‘and if none of you is indignant’, and κότῳ is ‘in resentment’ (κότος keeps the house word ‘resentment’). ἕκαστος ‘each one’ is nominative, in apposition to the ‘you’ of the verb. γενεῆφι has the epic ending -φι, here ‘in birth, in age’, and νεώτατος is ‘youngest’. The unit begins mid-line and closes at the ano teleia of line 112.

sentences.t:
πατρὸς δ’ ἐξ ἀγαθοῦ καὶ ἐγὼ γένος εὔχομαι εἶναι
Τυδέος, ὃν Θήβῃσι χυτὴ κατὰ γαῖα καλύπτει.
sentences.tr:
patros d’ ex agathou kai egō genos euchomai einai
Tydeos, hon Thēbēisi chytē kata gaia kalyptei.
sentences.l:
and from a father, a good one, I too my birth declare to be,
Tydeus, whom at Thebes the heaped earth covers over.
sentences.i: And I too declare my birth to be from a good father, Tydeus, whom the heaped earth covers at Thebes.
sentences.n: πατρὸς … ἐξ ἀγαθοῦ is ‘from a good father’, and Τυδέος (line 114) is the genitive naming him, in apposition to πατρός. γένος εὔχομαι εἶναι is ‘I declare my birth to be’: εὔχομαι takes the accusative γένος and the infinitive. Θήβῃσι is the locative dative plural, ‘at Thebes’, and χυτὴ γαῖα ‘heaped earth’ is the burial mound; κατά … καλύπτει is tmesis, the preverb standing apart from its verb, ‘covers over’.

sentences.t:
πορθεῖ γὰρ τρεῖς παῖδες ἀμύμονες ἐξεγένοντο,
οἴκεον δ’ ἐν Πλευρῶνι καὶ αἰπεινῇ Καλυδῶνι
Ἄγριος ἠδὲ Μέλας, τρίτατος δ’ ἦν ἱππότα Οἰνεὺς
πατρὸς ἐμοῖο πατήρ·
sentences.tr:
porthei gar treis paides amymones exegenonto,
oikeon d’ en Pleurōni kai aipeinēi Kalydōni
Agrios ēde Melas, tritatos d’ ēn hippota Oineus
patros emoio patēr·
sentences.l:
For to Portheus three sons, blameless, were born,
and they dwelt in Pleuron and in steep Calydon,
Agrius and Melas, and the third was Oeneus the horseman,
my father’s father;
sentences.i: For to Portheus three blameless sons were born, and they lived in Pleuron and steep Calydon, Agrius and Melas, and the third was Oeneus the horseman, my father’s father;
sentences.n: πορθεῖ is the dative of the name Portheus, printed here with a small letter, and ἐξεγένοντο ‘were born’ takes it: ‘to Portheus’. γάρ ‘for’ gives the ground of the claim to a good father: the family is now told. ἀμύμονες keeps the house rendering ‘blameless’, though the real sense of ἀμύμων is not known. οἴκεον is the uncontracted imperfect of οἰκέω ‘dwell’, and Ἄγριος ἠδὲ Μέλας, the first two sons, are its subject, placed after it; Pleuron and Calydon are towns of Aetolia. ἱππότα ‘horseman’ is the old nominative in -τα (Attic -της). πατρὸς ἐμοῖο is ‘of my father’, with ἐμοῖο the epic genitive of ἐμός, so Oeneus is Diomedes’ grandfather. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 118.

sentences.t: ἀρετῇ δ’ ἦν ἔξοχος αὐτῶν.
sentences.tr: aretēi d’ ēn exochos autōn.
sentences.l: and in excellence he was standing out above them.
sentences.i: and he stood out above them in excellence.
sentences.n: ἀρετῇ is a dative of respect, ‘in excellence’ (the word keeps ‘excellence’), and ἔξοχος αὐτῶν ‘standing out above them’ has the genitive of those surpassed, the three brothers. The unit begins mid-line, after the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὃ μὲν αὐτόθι μεῖνε, πατὴρ δ’ ἐμὸς Ἄργεϊ νάσθη
πλαγχθείς·
sentences.tr:
all’ ho men autothi meine, patēr d’ emos Argeï nasthē
planchtheis·
sentences.l:
But he, for his part, stayed there on the spot, and my father in Argos settled,
having wandered;
sentences.i: But Oeneus stayed where he was, while my father, after wandering, settled in Argos;
sentences.n: ὃ μὲν … πατὴρ δ’ ἐμός sets ‘the one’ against ‘my father’: ὃ μέν is Oeneus, who is just described as standing out, and the father is Tydeus. αὐτόθι is ‘on the spot, right there’. Ἄργεϊ is the locative dative of Ἄργος with the epic ending -εϊ, ‘in Argos’, and νάσθη is the aorist passive of ναίω ‘dwell’, here ‘settled’. πλαγχθείς ‘having been driven astray’ (πλάζω) says how Tydeus came to leave Aetolia. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t: ὡς γάρ που Ζεὺς ἤθελε καὶ θεοὶ ἄλλοι.
sentences.tr: hōs gar pou Zeus ēthele kai theoi alloi.
sentences.l: for so, doubtless, Zeus wished, and the other gods.
sentences.i: for so, doubtless, Zeus wished it, and the other gods.
sentences.n: ὡς … ἤθελε is ‘so he wished’: ὡς here is ‘so, thus’, and ἤθελε is the imperfect of ἐθέλω ‘wish’. που ‘doubtless’ makes the claim a supposition, and καὶ θεοὶ ἄλλοι ‘and the other gods’ joins Zeus as the cause of Tydeus’ wandering. The unit begins mid-line, after the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
Ἀδρήστοιο δ’ ἔγημε θυγατρῶν, ναῖε δὲ δῶμα
ἀφνειὸν βιότοιο, ἅλις δέ οἱ ἦσαν ἄρουραι
πυροφόροι, πολλοὶ δὲ φυτῶν ἔσαν ὄρχατοι ἀμφίς,
πολλὰ δέ οἱ πρόβατ’ ἔσκε·
sentences.tr:
Adrēstoio d’ egēme thygatrōn, naie de dōma
aphneion biotoio, halis de hoi ēsan arourai
pyrophoroi, polloi de phytōn esan orchatoi amphis,
polla de hoi probat’ eske·
sentences.l:
And of Adrastus’ daughters he married one, and dwelt in a house
rich in livelihood, and in plenty for him were fields,
wheat-bearing, and many orchards of trees there were all round,
and many flocks for him there used to be;
sentences.i: He married one of the daughters of Adrastus, and he lived in a house rich in livelihood, and he had wheat-bearing fields in plenty, and many orchards of trees all round, and many flocks;
sentences.n: The subject is now Tydeus, ‘my father’. Ἀδρήστοιο … θυγατρῶν is a partitive genitive, ‘[one] of the daughters of Adrastus’, and ἔγημε is the aorist of γαμέω ‘marry’, said of the man. δῶμα ἀφνειὸν βιότοιο is ‘a house rich in livelihood’: βιότοιο is a genitive of respect, and βίοτος means both ‘life’ and ‘means of living’, and here it is the second. ἅλις ‘in plenty’, ἄρουραι πυροφόροι ‘wheat-bearing fields’, ὄρχατοι ‘orchards’ (φυτῶν ‘of trees’, literally ‘of planted things’), ἀμφίς ‘all round’. πρόβατα ‘flocks’ is the general word for grazing stock, and the neuter plural takes the singular verb ἔσκε, an iterative form of εἰμί, ‘used to be’. ἔσαν is the Homeric imperfect 3rd plural (Attic ἦσαν). The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 124.

sentences.t:
κέκαστο δὲ πάντας Ἀχαιοὺς
ἐγχείῃ·
sentences.tr:
kekasto de pantas Achaious
encheiēi·
sentences.l:
and he had excelled all the Achaeans
with the spear;
sentences.i: and he had excelled all the Achaeans with the spear;
sentences.n: κέκαστο is the pluperfect of κέκασμαι ‘excel, surpass’ and takes the accusative of those surpassed, πάντας Ἀχαιούς. ἐγχείῃ is the dative of ἐγχείη, a by-form of ἔγχος, ‘with the spear’. The unit begins mid-line and ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: τὰ δὲ μέλλετ’ ἀκουέμεν, εἰ ἐτεόν περ.
sentences.tr: ta de mellet’ akouemen, ei eteon per.
sentences.l: and these things you are likely to hear, if it is true indeed.
sentences.i: and these are things you are likely to hear, if they are indeed true.
sentences.n: μέλλετ’ with the infinitive is ‘you are likely to’, and ἀκουέμεν is ἀκούειν with the epic infinitive ending -έμεν. εἰ ἐτεόν περ is ‘if it is true indeed’ (ἐτεόν is the neuter of ἐτεός ‘true’). The unit begins mid-line, after the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
τὼ οὐκ ἄν με γένος γε κακὸν καὶ ἀνάλκιδα φάντες
μῦθον ἀτιμήσαιτε πεφασμένον ὅν κ’ ἐῢ εἴπω.
sentences.tr:
tō ouk an me genos ge kakon kai analkida phantes
mython atimēsaite pephasmenon hon k’ eÿ eipō.
sentences.l:
Therefore not would you, me of birth base and without might
having called, dishonour a word spoken, which I may well speak.
sentences.i: So you would not, calling me base in birth and without might, dishonour the word that is spoken, if I speak it well.
sentences.n: τὼ (= τῷ) is ‘therefore’. οὐκ ἄν … ἀτιμήσαιτε is a potential optative, ‘you would not dishonour’. με is the object of φάντες, the aorist participle of φημί ‘say’, with γένος γε κακόν ‘base in birth’ (accusative of respect) and ἀνάλκιδα ‘without might’ (ἄναλκις; ἀλκή is ‘might’). μῦθον … πεφασμένον ‘a word spoken’, a perfect passive participle, is what they would dishonour, and the relative clause ὅν κ’ ἐῢ εἴπω ‘which I may well speak’ has κε with the subjunctive.

sentences.t: δεῦτ’ ἴομεν πόλεμον δὲ καὶ οὐτάμενοί περ ἀνάγκῃ.
sentences.tr: deut’ iomen polemon de kai outamenoi per anankēi.
sentences.l: Come, let us go to the war, even wounded though we be, by necessity.
sentences.i: Come, let us go to the war, wounded though we are, since we must.
sentences.n: δεῦτε is ‘come now’ (plural), and ἴομεν is the subjunctive of εἶμι, ‘let us go’. πόλεμον δέ is πόλεμόνδε written as two words: the suffix -δε gives direction, ‘to the war’. οὐτάμενοι ‘wounded’ (aorist participle of οὐτάω) with καί … περ ‘even though’ speaks of the wounded kings themselves. ἀνάγκῃ is the dative ‘by necessity’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δ’ ἔπειτ’ αὐτοὶ μὲν ἐχώμεθα δηϊοτῆτος
ἐκ βελέων, μή πού τις ἐφ’ ἕλκεϊ ἕλκος ἄρηται·
sentences.tr:
entha d’ epeit’ autoi men echōmetha dēïotētos
ek beleōn, mē pou tis eph’ helkeï helkos arētai·
sentences.l:
And there then let us ourselves, for our part, hold back from the fighting,
out of the shafts, lest anyhow someone upon a wound a wound take up;
sentences.i: And there, then, let us ourselves hold back from the fighting, out of the reach of the shafts, so that no one somehow takes wound upon wound;
sentences.n: ἔνθα ‘there’ is at the war. ἐχώμεθα is the middle subjunctive of ἔχω, ‘let us hold ourselves back’, with the genitive δηϊοτῆτος ‘from the fighting’ and ἐκ βελέων ‘out of the shafts’. μή πού τις introduces a fear, with ἄρηται, the aorist subjunctive of ἄρνυμαι ‘win, take for oneself’. ἐφ’ ἕλκεϊ ἕλκος is ‘wound upon wound’, ἕλκεϊ being the epic dative of ἕλκος. The unit ends at the ano teleia in line 130.

sentences.t:
ἄλλους δ’ ὀτρύνοντες ἐνήσομεν, οἳ τὸ πάρος περ
θυμῷ ἦρα φέροντες ἀφεστᾶσ’ οὐδὲ μάχονται.
sentences.tr:
allous d’ otrynontes enēsomen, hoi to paros per
thymōi ēra pherontes aphestas’ oude machontai.
sentences.l:
but others, urging them on, we shall send in, who before this, even,
to their heart bringing favour, stand aloof and do not fight.”
sentences.i: but we shall urge on the others and send them in, those who, indulging their hearts, have kept apart until now and do not fight.”
sentences.n: ἄλλους is the object of ὀτρύνοντες ‘urging on’ and ἐνήσομεν, the future of ἐνίημι ‘send in’: the wounded kings will not fight themselves but will push the others in. οἳ … ἀφεστᾶσ’ is ‘who stand aloof’ (ἀφεστᾶσ’ is the perfect of ἀφίσταμαι with the final -ι elided), and τὸ πάρος περ is ‘even before this’, ‘up to now’. θυμῷ ἦρα φέροντες is an idiom, ‘bringing favour to their heart’, that is, indulging their own wishes. This is the end of Diomedes’ speech.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἄρα τοῦ μάλα μὲν κλύον ἠδὲ πίθοντο·
sentences.tr: hōs ephath’, hoi d’ ara tou mala men klyon ēde pithonto·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they then readily heard him and obeyed.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they listened to him readily and obeyed.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ ‘so he spoke’ is the formula that closes a speech. οἳ δ’ ἄρα is ‘and they then’, with οἳ the pronoun, and κλύον is ἔκλυον ‘heard’ without the augment (here ‘listened to’), taking the genitive τοῦ ‘him’. πίθοντο is ἐπίθοντο ‘obeyed’, without the augment. μάλα μέν ‘readily’ looks forward to the ἠδέ ‘and’.

sentences.t: βὰν δ’ ἴμεν, ἦρχε δ’ ἄρά σφιν ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων.
sentences.tr: ban d’ imen, ērche d’ ara sphin anax andrōn Agamemnōn.
sentences.l: And they set out to go, and led them the lord of men, Agamemnon.
sentences.i: And they set out, and Agamemnon, lord of men, led them.
sentences.n: βὰν δ’ ἴμεν ‘they set out to go’ has βάν for ἔβησαν (3rd plural aorist, no augment) and ἴμεν for ἰέναι ‘to go’. ἦρχε ‘led’ takes the dative σφιν ‘them’. ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων is Agamemnon’s stock epithet, ‘lord of men’, translated every time.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἀλαοσκοπιὴν εἶχε κλυτὸς ἐννοσίγαιος,
ἀλλὰ μετ’ αὐτοὺς ἦλθε παλαιῷ φωτὶ ἐοικώς,
δεξιτερὴν δ’ ἕλε χεῖρ’ Ἀγαμέμνονος Ἀτρεΐδαο,
καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr:
oud’ alaoskopiēn eiche klytos ennosigaios,
alla met’ autous ēlthe palaiōi phōti eoikōs,
dexiterēn d’ hele cheir’ Agamemnonos Atreïdao,
kai min phōnēsas epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l:
Nor a blind man’s watch kept the famous earth-shaker,
but among them he went, to an old man likened,
and the right hand he took of Agamemnon, Atreus’-son,
and, lifting his voice, to him winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: Nor was the famous earth-shaker keeping a blind man’s watch, but he went among them looking like an old man, and took the right hand of Agamemnon, son of Atreus, and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: Poseidon is not named: κλυτὸς ἐννοσίγαιος ‘the famous earth-shaker’ is his epithet standing alone. οὐδ’ ἀλαοσκοπιὴν εἶχε ‘he kept no blind man’s watch’ is an idiom for a lookout that sees nothing (ἀλαός ‘blind’ + σκοπιή ‘watch’): he was not careless. παλαιῷ φωτὶ ἐοικώς ‘likened to an old man’ takes the dative: he comes in disguise. δεξιτερὴν … χεῖρ’ is the right hand, and Ἀτρεΐδαο the epic genitive in -αο. καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is the stock introduction, and here μιν is Agamemnon. The unit ends at the ano teleia at the end of line 138.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη νῦν δή που Ἀχιλλῆος ὀλοὸν κῆρ
γηθεῖ ἐνὶ στήθεσσι φόνον καὶ φύζαν Ἀχαιῶν
δερκομένῳ, ἐπεὶ οὔ οἱ ἔνι φρένες οὐδ’ ἠβαιαί.
sentences.tr:
Atreïdē nyn dē pou Achillēos oloon kēr
gēthei eni stēthessi phonon kai phyzan Achaiōn
derkomenōi, epei ou hoi eni phrenes oud’ ēbaiai.
sentences.l:
“Atreus’-son, now indeed, doubtless, of Achilles the deadly heart
rejoices in his breast, slaughter and the panic of the Achaeans
to him beholding, since in him are no wits, not even small ones.
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, now doubtless the deadly heart of Achilles rejoices in his breast, as he looks on the slaughter and the panic of the Achaeans, since there are no wits in him, not even small ones.
sentences.n: Ἀτρεΐδη is the vocative. νῦν δή που is ‘now indeed, doubtless’. Ἀχιλλῆος ὀλοὸν κῆρ ‘the deadly heart of Achilles’ is the subject of γηθεῖ (the third person singular of γηθέω ‘rejoice’), and φόνον καὶ φύζαν ‘slaughter and panic’ (φύζα is panic flight) are what it sees. δερκομένῳ is a dative participle, ‘to him looking on’, agreeing with an unstated ‘him’, Achilles, not with κῆρ. ἔνι is ἔνεστι ‘there is in’, with οἱ ‘in him’, and οὐδ’ ἠβαιαί is ‘not even small ones’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ὃ μὲν ὣς ἀπόλοιτο, θεὸς δέ ἑ σιφλώσειε·
sentences.tr: all’ ho men hōs apoloito, theos de he siphlōseie·
sentences.l: but let him thus perish, and may a god maim him;
sentences.i: But let him perish so, and may a god maim him;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὃ μέν ‘but he for his part’ is Achilles, and ὣς is ‘so, thus’. ἀπόλοιτο and σιφλώσειε are aorist optatives of wish, with ἑ ‘him’ the object of the second. The meaning of σιφλώσειε is not certain: ‘maim’ is the usual guess.

sentences.t:
σοὶ δ’ οὔ πω μάλα πάγχυ θεοὶ μάκαρες κοτέουσιν,
ἀλλ’ ἔτι που Τρώων ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες
εὐρὺ κονίσουσιν πεδίον, σὺ δ’ ἐπόψεαι αὐτὸς
φεύγοντας προτὶ ἄστυ νεῶν ἄπο καὶ κλισιάων.
sentences.tr:
soi d’ ou pō mala panchy theoi makares koteousin,
all’ eti pou Trōōn hēgētores ēde medontes
eury konisousin pedion, sy d’ epopseai autos
pheugontas proti asty neōn apo kai klisiaōn.
sentences.l:
but with you not yet quite utterly do the blessed gods bear a grudge,
but still, doubtless, of the Trojans the leaders and lords
will raise dust on the wide plain, and you yourself will look upon them
fleeing toward the city, away from the ships and the huts.”
sentences.i: But the blessed gods do not yet bear a grudge against you altogether; the leaders and lords of the Trojans will still, doubtless, raise the dust on the wide plain, and you yourself will look upon them fleeing toward the city, away from the ships and the huts.”
sentences.n: σοί ‘with you’ is the dative of the person the grudge is held against (κοτέουσιν ‘bear a grudge’); οὔ πω μάλα πάγχυ is ‘not yet altogether’. Τρώων ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες ‘leaders and lords of the Trojans’ is a formula. εὐρὺ … πεδίον is the wide plain, κονίσουσιν the future of κονίω ‘raise dust’. ἐπόψεαι is the future of ἐφοράω ‘look upon’, with the epic ending -εαι (Attic -ῃ), and φεύγοντας is ‘them fleeing’. προτί is πρός, and νεῶν ἄπο is ἀπὸ νεῶν, the preposition after its noun; κλισιάων is the epic genitive plural of κλισίη ‘hut’. This is the end of Poseidon’s speech.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν μέγ’ ἄϋσεν ἐπεσσύμενος πεδίοιο.
sentences.tr: hōs eipōn meg’ aÿsen epessymenos pedioio.
sentences.l: So having spoken, loudly he shouted, rushing over the plain.
sentences.i: So saying, he shouted loudly as he rushed over the plain.
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών ‘so saying’ closes the speech. The subject is still Poseidon, unnamed. μέγα is adverbial, ‘loudly’, ἄϋσεν is the aorist of ἀΰω ‘shout’, and ἐπεσσύμενος ‘rushing on’ is the participle of ἐπισεύομαι with the doubled σ. πεδίοιο is the genitive of the ground crossed, ‘over the plain’.

sentences.t:
ὅσσόν τ’ ἐννεάχιλοι ἐπίαχον ἢ δεκάχιλοι
ἀνέρες ἐν πολέμῳ ἔριδα ξυνάγοντες Ἄρηος,
sentences.tr:
hosson t’ enneachiloi epiachon ē dekachiloi
aneres en polemōi erida xynagontes Arēos,
sentences.l:
as loud as nine-thousand or ten-thousand shout
men in war, joining the strife of Ares,
sentences.i: As loud as nine thousand or ten thousand men cry out in war, when they join in the strife of war,
sentences.n: ὅσσον … τόσσην ‘as loud as … so great (a voice)’ sets Poseidon’s shout against that of a crowd: ἐννεάχιλοι ἢ δεκάχιλοι ‘nine-thousand or ten-thousand (men)’ is a figure for a great number, not a count, and ἔριδα … Ἄρηος ‘the strife of Ares’ puts the god’s name for war. ἐπίαχον is ‘shouted’. The English of these two lines is that of the same lines at 5.860–861. The unit ends at the comma after Ἄρηος, and the comparison is finished in the next unit, which begins with τόσσην.

sentences.t:
τόσσην ἐκ στήθεσφιν ὄπα κρείων ἐνοσίχθων
ἧκεν· Ἀχαιοῖσιν δὲ μέγα σθένος ἔμβαλ’ ἑκάστῳ
καρδίῃ, ἄληκτον πολεμίζειν ἠδὲ μάχεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
tossēn ek stēthesphin opa kreiōn enosichthōn
hēken· Achaioisin de mega sthenos embal’ hekastōi
kardiēi, alēkton polemizein ēde machesthai.
sentences.l:
so great a voice from his chest the lord earth-shaker
sent forth; and to the Achaeans great strength he put, to each
in the heart, unrelenting, to make war and to fight.
sentences.i: so great a voice did the lord earth-shaker send forth from his chest; and he put great, relentless strength into the heart of every Achaean, for making war and fighting.
sentences.n: τόσσην … ἧκεν ‘so great a voice … sent forth’ completes the comparison: ὄπα is the accusative of ὄψ ‘voice’, and ἐκ στήθεσφιν has the epic ending -φιν, ‘from his chest’. κρείων ἐνοσίχθων ‘the lord earth-shaker’ is Poseidon by epithet alone, and ἧκεν is ‘sent forth’. The unit goes on after the ano teleia in mid-line 151: Ἀχαιοῖσιν … ἑκάστῳ ‘to the Achaeans, to each’ (ἑκάστῳ is masculine and goes with the people, not with καρδίῃ), and καρδίῃ ‘in the heart’ is a dative of place. ἔμβαλ’ is ἐνέβαλε ‘put in’, and ἄληκτον ‘unceasing’, here ‘unrelenting’, agrees with σθένος ‘strength’. πολεμίζειν ἠδὲ μάχεσθαι ‘to make war and to fight’ say what the strength is for. The subject is Poseidon.

sentences.t:
Ἥρη δ’ εἰσεῖδε χρυσόθρονος ὀφθαλμοῖσι
στᾶσ’ ἐξ Οὐλύμποιο ἀπὸ ῥίου·
sentences.tr:
Hērē d’ eiseide chrysothronos ophthalmoisi
stas’ ex Oulympoio apo rhiou·
sentences.l:
And Hera looked, golden-throned, with her eyes,
standing from Olympus, from a peak;
sentences.i: And golden-throned Hera, standing on a peak of Olympus, looked on with her eyes;
sentences.n: The scene changes to Olympus. χρυσόθρονος ‘golden-throned’ is Hera’s stock epithet (some in antiquity took the second part from θρόνα ‘embroidered flowers’). εἰσεῖδε ‘looked at’ has no object yet, and the next unit gives it. ὀφθαλμοῖσι is ‘with her eyes’. στᾶσ’ is the aorist participle of ἵστημι, ‘having taken her stand’, and ἐξ Οὐλύμποιο ἀπὸ ῥίου is ‘from Olympus, from a peak’ (ῥίον ‘peak’), the place she looks from. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 154.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα δ’ ἔγνω
τὸν μὲν ποιπνύοντα μάχην ἀνὰ κυδιάνειραν
αὐτοκασίγνητον καὶ δαέρα, χαῖρε δὲ θυμῷ·
sentences.tr:
autika d’ egnō
ton men poipnyonta machēn ana kydianeiran
autokasignēton kai daera, chaire de thymōi·
sentences.i: and at once she knew him, bustling through the battle that brings men glory, her own brother and her husband’s brother, and she rejoiced in her heart;
sentences.n: αὐτίκα δ’ ἔγνω ‘and at once she recognized’; τὸν μέν ‘him’, Poseidon, is set against Ζῆνα δέ ‘but Zeus’ in the next unit. ποιπνύοντα ‘bustling’ and μάχην ἀνὰ κυδιάνειραν ‘through the man-glorifying battle’ (‘the battle that brings men glory’). αὐτοκασίγνητον καὶ δαέρα says that he is both her own brother and her husband’s brother, δαέρα being the accusative of δαήρ ‘husband’s brother’. The unit begins mid-line, after the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
Ζῆνα δ’ ἐπ’ ἀκροτάτης κορυφῆς πολυπίδακος Ἴδης
ἥμενον εἰσεῖδε, στυγερὸς δέ οἱ ἔπλετο θυμῷ.
sentences.tr:
Zēna d’ ep’ akrotatēs koryphēs polypidakos Idēs
hēmenon eiseide, stygeros de hoi epleto thymōi.
sentences.l:
and Zeus on the topmost peak of many-springed Ida
sitting she looked at, and hateful to her he was in her heart.
sentences.i: and she saw Zeus sitting on the topmost peak of many-springed Ida, and he was hateful to her in her heart.
sentences.n: Ζῆνα is the accusative of Ζεύς. ἀκροτάτης κορυφῆς is ‘the topmost peak’, and πολυπίδακος ‘with many springs’ (πίδαξ ‘spring’) is the stock epithet of Ida, the mountain above Troy. ἥμενον is ‘sitting’, and εἰσεῖδε repeats the verb of line 153: she looked at Poseidon, and then at Zeus. στυγερὸς … οἱ ἔπλετο θυμῷ is ‘he was hateful to her in her heart’, with οἱ ‘to her’.

sentences.t:
μερμήριξε δ’ ἔπειτα βοῶπις πότνια Ἥρη
ὅππως ἐξαπάφοιτο Διὸς νόον αἰγιόχοιο·
sentences.tr:
mermērixe d’ epeita boōpis potnia Hērē
hoppōs exapaphoito Dios noon aigiochoio·
sentences.l:
And then she pondered, ox-eyed lady Hera,
how she might cheat the mind of aegis-bearing Zeus;
sentences.i: And then ox-eyed lady Hera pondered how she might cheat the mind of aegis-bearing Zeus;
sentences.n: μερμήριξε ‘pondered’ is followed by a clause with ὅππως ‘how’ and the aorist optative ἐξαπάφοιτο ‘she might cheat’ (ἐξαπαφίσκω), with Διὸς νόον ‘the mind of Zeus’ as its object. βοῶπις ‘ox-eyed’ (usually explained as large, calm eyes) and πότνια ‘lady’ are Hera’s stock epithets, and αἰγιόχοιο ‘aegis-bearing’ is Zeus’s (meaning disputed, usually ‘holding the αἰγίς’).

sentences.t:
ἥδε δέ οἱ κατὰ θυμὸν ἀρίστη φαίνετο βουλὴ
ἐλθεῖν εἰς Ἴδην εὖ ἐντύνασαν ἓ αὐτήν,
sentences.tr:
hēde de hoi kata thymon aristē phaineto boulē
elthein eis Idēn eu entynasan he autēn,
sentences.l:
And this seemed to her in her heart the best plan,
to go to Ida, having well arrayed herself,
sentences.i: And this seemed to her in her heart the best plan: to go to Ida, once she had arrayed herself well,
sentences.n: ἥδε … ἀρίστη … βουλή is ‘this best plan’ (ἥδε is the demonstrative ‘this’). κατὰ θυμόν is ‘in her heart’, and φαίνετο ‘seemed’. ἐλθεῖν is the infinitive that says what the plan was. ἐντύνασαν is the feminine accusative aorist participle of ἐντύνω ‘array, make ready’, agreeing with the unstated ‘her’ that is the subject of ἐλθεῖν, and ἓ αὐτήν is ‘herself’ (ἕ the reflexive, αὐτήν for emphasis).

sentences.t:
εἴ πως ἱμείραιτο παραδραθέειν φιλότητι
ᾗ χροιῇ, τῷ δ’ ὕπνον ἀπήμονά τε λιαρόν τε
χεύῃ ἐπὶ βλεφάροισιν ἰδὲ φρεσὶ πευκαλίμῃσι.
sentences.tr:
ei pōs himeiraito paradratheein philotēti
hēi chroiēi, tōi d’ hypnon apēmona te liaron te
cheuēi epi blepharoisin ide phresi peukalimēisi.
sentences.l:
if somehow he might long to lie beside her in love
with her own skin, and on him sleep, harmless and warm,
she might pour upon his eyelids and his keen wits.
sentences.i: in case he might long to lie beside her in love, with her own body, and she might pour on him a sleep, harmless and warm, over his eyelids and his keen wits.
sentences.n: εἴ πως ‘in case somehow’ governs two verbs with different subjects, and the Greek does not mark the change: ἱμείραιτο ‘he might long’ (Zeus), then χεύῃ ‘she might pour’ (Hera, aorist of χέω). παραδραθέειν is the aorist infinitive ‘to lie beside’, φιλότητι ‘in love’. ᾗ is the possessive ‘her own’, not the relative, with χροιῇ ‘skin’ in the dative of means, that is, her body. τῷ is ‘on him’, and ἀπήμονά τε λιαρόν τε ‘harmless and warm’ describes the sleep. ἰδέ is ‘and’. πευκαλίμῃσι ‘keen’ is the traditional sense; its formation is not certain.

sentences.t:
βῆ δ’ ἴμεν ἐς θάλαμον, τόν οἱ φίλος υἱὸς ἔτευξεν
Ἥφαιστος, πυκινὰς δὲ θύρας σταθμοῖσιν ἐπῆρσε
κληῗδι κρυπτῇ, τὴν δ’ οὐ θεὸς ἄλλος ἀνῷγεν·
sentences.tr:
bē d’ imen es thalamon, ton hoi philos huios eteuxen
Hēphaistos, pykinas de thyras stathmoisin epērse
klēïdi kryptēi, tēn d’ ou theos allos anōigen·
sentences.i: She set out for the chamber that her dear son Hephaestus had made for her, and he had fitted close-fitting doors to its doorposts with a hidden bolt, which no other god opened;
sentences.n: βῆ δ’ ἴμεν ‘she set out to go’. τόν is the relative ‘which’, referring to θάλαμον ‘chamber’, and οἱ is ‘for her’; Hephaestus is Hera’s own son. πυκινὰς … θύρας is ‘close-fitting doors’ (πυκινός ‘close, solid’), ἐπῆρσε ‘fitted’, σταθμοῖσιν ‘to the doorposts’. κληῗδι κρυπτῇ is ‘with a hidden bolt’, and τὴν is the bolt as the object of ἀνῷγεν, the augmented imperfect of ἀνοίγω ‘open’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: ἔνθ’ ἥ γ’ εἰσελθοῦσα θύρας ἐπέθηκε φαεινάς.
sentences.tr: enth’ hē g’ eiselthousa thyras epethēke phaeinas.
sentences.l: There she, having gone in, put to the shining doors.
sentences.i: There, once she had gone in, she shut the shining doors.
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ ‘there’ and ἥ γ’ ‘she’ (the pronoun) pick up Hera. εἰσελθοῦσα is ‘having gone in’, ἐπέθηκε θύρας ‘put the doors to’, that is, shut them, and φαεινάς is ‘shining’.

sentences.t:
ἀμβροσίῃ μὲν πρῶτον ἀπὸ χροὸς ἱμερόεντος
λύματα πάντα κάθηρεν, ἀλείψατο δὲ λίπ’ ἐλαίῳ
ἀμβροσίῳ ἑδανῷ, τό ῥά οἱ τεθυωμένον ἦεν·
sentences.tr:
ambrosiēi men prōton apo chroos himeroentos
lymata panta kathēren, aleipsato de lip’ elaiōi
ambrosiōi hedanōi, to rha hoi tethyōmenon ēen·
sentences.i: First she cleansed all the filth from her skin, full of longing, with ambrosia, and she anointed herself richly with ambrosial oil, sweet, which had been perfumed for her;
sentences.n: ἀμβροσίῃ is ambrosia, the gods’ own substance, here used as a cleanser, and ἀμβρόσιος ‘ambrosial’ is the adjective for what belongs to it (ἀ- + βροτός ‘deathless’). χροὸς ἱμερόεντος is ‘her skin full of longing’, the epithet naming what the sight of it stirs. λύματα ‘filth’ is what is washed off, and κάθηρεν is the aorist of καθαίρω, here without the augment. ἀλείψατο ‘anointed herself’, λίπ’ ἐλαίῳ ‘richly with oil’ (λίπα is an adverb, ‘richly, sleekly’). ἑδανῷ ‘sweet’ is the traditional sense and is not certain. τεθυωμένον is the perfect passive participle of θυόω, ‘perfumed’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
τοῦ καὶ κινυμένοιο Διὸς κατὰ χαλκοβατὲς δῶ
ἔμπης ἐς γαῖάν τε καὶ οὐρανὸν ἵκετ’ ἀϋτμή.
sentences.tr:
tou kai kinymenoio Dios kata chalkobates dō
empēs es gaian te kai ouranon hiket’ aÿtmē.
sentences.l:
Of it, even when stirred in the house of Zeus, the bronze-floored,
all the same to earth and heaven came the scent.
sentences.i: Even when it was stirred in the house of Zeus with the bronze floor, its scent all the same reached earth and heaven.
sentences.n: τοῦ is ‘of it’, the oil, and goes with ἀϋτμή ‘scent’ (literally ‘breath, vapour’), the subject, which stands last. κινυμένοιο ‘when it was stirred’ is the participle of κινύομαι. Διὸς κατὰ χαλκοβατὲς δῶ is ‘down in the bronze-floored house of Zeus’: δῶ is short for δῶμα, and χαλκοβατές ‘bronze-floored’ may mean floor or threshold (disputed). ἔμπης ‘all the same’, and ἵκετ’ is ἵκετο ‘reached’.

sentences.t:
τῷ ῥ’ ἥ γε χρόα καλὸν ἀλειψαμένη ἰδὲ χαίτας
πεξαμένη χερσὶ πλοκάμους ἔπλεξε φαεινοὺς
καλοὺς ἀμβροσίους ἐκ κράατος ἀθανάτοιο.
sentences.tr:
tōi rh’ hē ge chroa kalon aleipsamenē ide chaitas
pexamenē chersi plokamous eplexe phaeinous
kalous ambrosious ek kraatos athanatoio.
sentences.l:
With this, having anointed her fine skin, and her hair
having combed with her hands, she plaited the locks, shining,
fine, ambrosial, from her immortal head.
sentences.i: With it she anointed her fine skin, and she combed her hair with her hands and plaited her shining, fine, ambrosial locks from her immortal head.
sentences.n: τῷ is ‘with this’, the oil. χρόα καλόν ‘fine skin’ is the accusative of χρώς, object of ἀλειψαμένη ‘having anointed’. ἰδὲ χαίτας πεξαμένη χερσί is ‘and having combed her hair with her hands’ (πεξαμένη is the aorist middle participle of πέκτω ‘comb’), and ἔπλεξε πλοκάμους ‘plaited her locks’. φαεινούς, καλούς, ἀμβροσίους are three adjectives, ‘shining, fine, ambrosial’. κράατος is an old genitive of κάρη ‘head’.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρ’ ἀμβρόσιον ἑανὸν ἕσαθ’, ὅν οἱ Ἀθήνη
ἔξυσ’ ἀσκήσασα, τίθει δ’ ἐνὶ δαίδαλα πολλά·
sentences.tr:
amphi d’ ar’ ambrosion heanon hesath’, hon hoi Athēnē
exys’ askēsasa, tithei d’ eni daidala polla·
sentences.l:
and about her an ambrosial fine robe she put on, which for her Athena
had smoothed, having worked it, and she set in it many intricate works;
sentences.i: She put on a fine, ambrosial robe, which Athena had worked and smoothed for her, setting many intricate works in it;
sentences.n: ἀμφὶ δ’ ‘and about (her)’; ἕσαθ’ is the aorist middle of ἕννυμι ‘put on’. ἀμβρόσιον ἑανόν is ‘a fine, ambrosial robe’: ἑανός ‘fine’ is not certain in sense (‘soft, light’), and here it stands for the robe itself. ὅν is the relative ‘which’, not the possessive, and οἱ is ‘for her’. ἔξυσ’ is the aorist of ξύω ‘scrape, smooth’, ἀσκήσασα ‘having worked it with skill’ (ἀσκέω), and τίθει is an unaugmented imperfect, ‘was setting’. δαίδαλα πολλά are ‘many intricate works’, the designs in the cloth.

sentences.t: χρυσείῃς δ’ ἐνετῇσι κατὰ στῆθος περονᾶτο.
sentences.tr: chryseiēis d’ enetēisi kata stēthos peronato.
sentences.l: and with golden pins on her breast she fastened it.
sentences.i: and she fastened it at her breast with golden pins.
sentences.n: χρυσείῃς … ἐνετῇσι is ‘with golden pins’ (ἐνετή ‘pin, brooch’; χρυσείῃς is the dative plural, = χρυσείαις). κατὰ στῆθος is ‘down over the breast’, and περονᾶτο is the imperfect middle of περονάω ‘fasten with a pin’, ‘she was fastening it for herself’; the robe of the previous line is the unstated object.

sentences.t:
ζώσατο δὲ ζώνῃ ἑκατὸν θυσάνοις ἀραρυίῃ,
ἐν δ’ ἄρα ἕρματα ἧκεν ἐϋτρήτοισι λοβοῖσι
τρίγληνα μορόεντα·
sentences.tr:
zōsato de zōnēi hekaton thysanois araruiēi,
en d’ ara hermata hēken eÿtrētoisi loboisi
triglēna moroenta·
sentences.i: She girded herself with a girdle fitted with a hundred tassels, and put earrings with three drops, mulberry-like, in her well-pierced ear-lobes;
sentences.n: ζώσατο ‘girded herself’ is the aorist middle of ζώννυμι, and ζώνῃ is the girdle, dative of means. ἑκατὸν θυσάνοις ἀραρυίῃ is ‘fitted with a hundred tassels’ (ἀραρυίῃ is the perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit’; a hundred is a round number for many). ἐν … ἧκεν is tmesis, ‘put in’. ἕρματα means earrings here (the word also means ‘props’), and ἐϋτρήτοισι λοβοῖσι is ‘in the well-pierced lobes’. The sense of τρίγληνα μορόεντα ‘three-eyed, mulberry-like’ is not certain in either word, as at Odyssey 18.298. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 183.

sentences.t: χάρις δ’ ἀπελάμπετο πολλή.
sentences.tr: charis d’ apelampeto pollē.
sentences.l: and grace shone forth from her, abundant.
sentences.i: and abundant grace shone forth from her.
sentences.n: χάρις is ‘grace, charm’, the beauty that shone from her adorned body; ἀπελάμπετο ‘shone forth’ is the imperfect (middle form) of ἀπολάμπω, and πολλή ‘abundant’ agrees with χάρις. The unit begins mid-line, after the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
κρηδέμνῳ δ’ ἐφύπερθε καλύψατο δῖα θεάων
καλῷ νηγατέῳ·
sentences.tr:
krēdemnōi d’ ephyperthe kalypsato dia theaōn
kalōi nēgateōi·
sentences.l:
and with a veil above she covered herself, heavenly-one of goddesses,
fine, new-made;
sentences.i: and she covered herself above with a fine, newly made veil, heavenly even among goddesses;
sentences.n: κρηδέμνῳ is the dative of κρήδεμνον ‘veil’, and ἐφύπερθε ‘above’ says where it lay. καλύψατο is the aorist middle ‘covered herself’. δῖα θεάων is ‘heavenly even among goddesses’ (literally ‘heavenly one of goddesses’). καλῷ νηγατέῳ is ‘fine, new-made’: ‘newly made’ is an ancient gloss, and the formation of νηγάτεος is not known. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 185.

sentences.t: λευκὸν δ’ ἦν ἠέλιος ὥς·
sentences.tr: leukon d’ ēn ēelios hōs·
sentences.l: and it was white as the sun;
sentences.i: and it was as white as the sun;
sentences.n: λευκόν is neuter, agreeing with κρηδέμνῳ, so the subject is the veil. ἠέλιος is the Homeric form of ἥλιος ‘sun’, and ὥς ‘as, like’ comes after its noun. The unit begins mid-line, after the ano teleia.

sentences.t: ποσσὶ δ’ ὑπὸ λιπαροῖσιν ἐδήσατο καλὰ πέδιλα.
sentences.tr: possi d’ hypo liparoisin edēsato kala pedila.
sentences.l: and under her sleek feet she bound fine sandals.
sentences.i: and she bound fine sandals beneath her sleek feet.
sentences.n: This is a stock line of dressing, used here of a goddess. ποσσί is the epic dative plural of πούς, λιπαροῖσιν ‘sleek’ (the oiled look of the skin), ἐδήσατο ‘bound on for herself’, and καλὰ πέδιλα ‘fine sandals’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δὴ πάντα περὶ χροῒ θήκατο κόσμον
βῆ ῥ’ ἴμεν ἐκ θαλάμοιο, καλεσσαμένη δ’ Ἀφροδίτην
τῶν ἄλλων ἀπάνευθε θεῶν πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπε·
sentences.tr:
autar epei dē panta peri chroï thēkato kosmon
bē rh’ imen ek thalamoio, kalessamenē d’ Aphroditēn
tōn allōn apaneuthe theōn pros mython eeipe·
sentences.l:
But when she had put all the adornment about her skin,
she set out to go from the chamber, and, having called Aphrodite
away from the other gods, she addressed her with a word:
sentences.i: But when she had put all the adornment about her body, she set out from the chamber, and, calling Aphrodite apart from the other gods, spoke to her:
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δή is ‘but when now’, and πάντα … κόσμον ‘all the adornment’ is the object of θήκατο ‘put on’ (aorist middle), with χροΐ the dative of χρώς, ‘about her skin’. βῆ ῥ’ ἴμεν ‘she set out to go’. καλεσσαμένη is ‘having called’, and ἀπάνευθε ‘apart from’ takes the genitive τῶν ἄλλων … θεῶν. πρὸς … ἔειπε is tmesis: ‘addressed with a word’ (μῦθον).

sentences.l:
“Would you now, then, obey me in something, dear child, whatever I may say,
or would you refuse, bearing a grudge in your heart over this,
because I help the Danaans, and you the Trojans?”
sentences.i: “Would you obey me now in something, dear child, whatever I tell you, or would you refuse, bearing a grudge in your heart over this, because I help the Danaans and you help the Trojans?”
sentences.n: ἦ ῥά νύ opens the question, ‘would you now, then’. πίθοιο is the optative of πείθομαι, ‘would you obey’, with μοι ‘me’ and τι ‘in something’, and ὅττί κεν εἴπω is ‘whatever I may say’ (ὅττι = ὅ τι, κεν with the subjunctive). φίλον τέκος ‘dear child’ is the address. ἀρνήσαιο is ‘would you refuse’, and κοτεσσαμένη is the aorist middle participle of κοτέω ‘bear a grudge’, with τό γε ‘over this’ and θυμῷ ‘in your heart’. In οὕνεκ’ ἐγὼ Δαναοῖσι, σὺ δὲ Τρώεσσιν ἀρήγεις ἐγώ has no verb of its own: ἀρήγεις is second person (‘you help’), so ‘I help’ is understood from it.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα Διὸς θυγάτηρ Ἀφροδίτη·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ ēmeibet’ epeita Dios thygatēr Aphroditē·
sentences.l: Her then answered the daughter of Zeus, Aphrodite:
sentences.i: Then Aphrodite, the daughter of Zeus, answered her:
sentences.n: τὴν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα is the reply-formula, ‘her then answered’ (ἠμείβετ’ is the imperfect of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer’, and τήν is Hera, its object), and Διὸς θυγάτηρ ‘the daughter of Zeus’ stands with Aphrodite’s name.

sentences.t:
Ἥρη πρέσβα θεὰ θύγατερ μεγάλοιο Κρόνοιο
αὔδα ὅ τι φρονέεις·
sentences.tr:
Hērē presba thea thygater megaloio Kronoio
auda ho ti phroneeis·
sentences.l:
“Hera, august goddess, daughter of great Cronus,
speak what you have in mind;
sentences.i: “Hera, august goddess, daughter of great Cronus, speak what you have in mind;
sentences.n: Ἥρη πρέσβα θεά is address: πρέσβα here is a title of honour, ‘august’ (the word can also mean ‘eldest’). θύγατερ μεγάλοιο Κρόνοιο is ‘daughter of great Cronus’, with the epic genitive in -οιο. αὔδα is the imperative of αὐδάω ‘speak out’, and ὅ τι φρονέεις ‘what you have in mind’ has the uncontracted φρονέεις (Attic φρονεῖς). The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
τελέσαι δέ με θυμὸς ἄνωγεν,
εἰ δύναμαι τελέσαι γε καὶ εἰ τετελεσμένον ἐστίν.
sentences.tr:
telesai de me thymos anōgen,
ei dynamai telesai ge kai ei tetelesmenon estin.
sentences.l:
and to accomplish it my heart bids me,
if I am able to accomplish it, and if it is a thing accomplishable.”
sentences.i: and my heart urges me to do it, if I can, and if it is a thing that is meant to be done.”
sentences.n: τελέσαι δέ με θυμὸς ἄνωγεν is ‘and my heart bids me to accomplish it’: ἄνωγεν is a perfect with present sense, ‘bids’, and the thing to be accomplished is what Hera has in mind. τετελεσμένον is the perfect passive participle of τελέω, here ‘able to be accomplished’. The same two lines stand in the Odyssey (5.89–90), and the English is the same. This is the end of Aphrodite’s speech.

sentences.t: τὴν δὲ δολοφρονέουσα προσηύδα πότνια Ἥρη·
sentences.tr: tēn de dolophroneousa prosēuda potnia Hērē·
sentences.l: And to her, with guile in her mind, spoke lady Hera:
sentences.i: Then lady Hera, with guile in her mind, spoke to her:
sentences.n: δολοφρονέουσα ‘with guile in her mind’ (an uncontracted participle, δόλος + φρονέω) is the poet’s warning: what Hera now says to Aphrodite is not her real purpose. προσηύδα ‘spoke to’ takes τήν ‘her’ as its object, and πότνια ‘lady’ is Hera’s stock epithet.

sentences.t:
δὸς νῦν μοι φιλότητα καὶ ἵμερον, ᾧ τε σὺ πάντας
δαμνᾷ ἀθανάτους ἠδὲ θνητοὺς ἀνθρώπους.
sentences.tr:
dos nyn moi philotēta kai himeron, hōi te sy pantas
damnāi athanatous ēde thnētous anthrōpous.
sentences.l:
“Give me now love and longing, with which you
subdue all the immortals and mortal men.
sentences.i: “Give me now the love and longing with which you subdue all the immortals and mortal men.
sentences.n: δός is the aorist imperative of δίδωμι ‘give’, and φιλότητα καὶ ἵμερον ‘love and longing’ are the powers that Aphrodite has. ᾧ is the relative, a dative of means, ‘with which’, and τε is the epic τε of a general truth. δαμνᾷ is the second person singular present of δάμνημι ‘subdue’. ἀθανάτους ἠδὲ θνητοὺς ἀνθρώπους is ‘the immortals and mortal men’.

sentences.t:
εἶμι γὰρ ὀψομένη πολυφόρβου πείρατα γαίης,
Ὠκεανόν τε θεῶν γένεσιν καὶ μητέρα Τηθύν,
sentences.tr:
eimi gar opsomenē polyphorbou peirata gaiēs,
Ōkeanon te theōn genesin kai mētera Tēthyn,
sentences.l:
For I am going to see the ends of the much-nourishing earth,
and Oceanus, the origin of the gods, and mother Tethys,
sentences.i: For I am going to see the ends of the much-nourishing earth, and Oceanus, the origin of the gods, and mother Tethys,
sentences.n: εἶμι ‘I am going’ is the present of εἶμι, and ὀψομένη ‘to see’ is a future participle of purpose. γάρ gives the reason for the request. πολυφόρβου … γαίης is ‘the much-nourishing earth’, and πείρατα ‘ends, limits’. Ὠκεανόν τε θεῶν γένεσιν καὶ μητέρα Τηθύν is ‘Oceanus, the origin of the gods, and mother Tethys’: the two are a married pair, as the later lines show.

sentences.t:
οἵ μ’ ἐν σφοῖσι δόμοισιν ἐῢ τρέφον ἠδ’ ἀτίταλλον
δεξάμενοι Ῥείας, ὅτε τε Κρόνον εὐρύοπα Ζεὺς
γαίης νέρθε καθεῖσε καὶ ἀτρυγέτοιο θαλάσσης·
sentences.tr:
hoi m’ en sphoisi domoisin eÿ trephon ēd’ atitallon
dexamenoi Rheias, hote te Kronon euryopa Zeus
gaiēs nerthe katheise kai atrygetoio thalassēs·
sentences.i: who raised and fostered me well in their own halls, when they took me in from Rhea, at the time when Zeus who thunders from afar set Cronus down below the earth and the sea that yields no harvest;
sentences.n: οἵ ‘who’ is the pair, and σφοῖσι δόμοισιν is ‘their own houses’ (σφός is the possessive ‘their own’, not a relative). ἐῢ τρέφον ἠδ’ ἀτίταλλον is ‘nourished well and fostered’, two imperfects. δεξάμενοι Ῥείας is ‘having received (me) from Rhea’, with the genitive of source. In ὅτε τε Κρόνον εὐρύοπα Ζεὺς … καθεῖσε the object is Cronus and the subject Zeus, εὐρύοπα ‘far-thundering’ being his stock epithet, and καθεῖσε is the aorist of καθίζω ‘seat’, used of putting a person in a place, ‘set down’; γαίης νέρθε is ‘beneath the earth’. ἀτρυγέτοιο ‘unharvested’ is the traditional sense of this stock epithet of the sea, but its real meaning is not known. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: τοὺς εἶμ’ ὀψομένη, καί σφ’ ἄκριτα νείκεα λύσω·
sentences.tr: tous eim’ opsomenē, kai sph’ akrita neikea lysō·
sentences.l: them I am going to see, and their unsorted quarrels I shall loose;
sentences.i: I am going to see them, and I shall settle their endless quarrels;
sentences.n: τοὺς ‘them’ is the article as a pronoun, the pair named above, and εἶμ’ ὀψομένη repeats ‘I am going to see’ of line 200. σφε is ‘them’. ἄκριτα νείκεα ‘unsorted quarrels’ (ἄκριτος, ‘not sorted out’, so ‘endless’) are what she says she will loose, as a knot is loosed; λύσω is the future of λύω.

sentences.t:
ἤδη γὰρ δηρὸν χρόνον ἀλλήλων ἀπέχονται
εὐνῆς καὶ φιλότητος, ἐπεὶ χόλος ἔμπεσε θυμῷ.
sentences.tr:
ēdē gar dēron chronon allēlōn apechontai
eunēs kai philotētos, epei cholos empese thymōi.
sentences.l:
for already for a long time from one another they have kept away,
from bed and from love, since anger fell upon their heart.
sentences.i: For they have already been keeping away from one another for a long time, from bed and from love, since anger fell upon their hearts.
sentences.n: ἤδη γάρ gives the reason: the quarrel is old. ἀπέχονται ‘keep away from’ takes the genitive, here ἀλλήλων ‘from one another’ and εὐνῆς καὶ φιλότητος ‘from bed and from love’. ἔμπεσε is the aorist of ἐμπίπτω ‘fall upon’, with θυμῷ ‘heart’ (singular, for both), and χόλος ‘anger’ keeps its house word.

sentences.t:
εἰ κείνω ἐπέεσσι παραιπεπιθοῦσα φίλον κῆρ
εἰς εὐνὴν ἀνέσαιμι ὁμωθῆναι φιλότητι,
αἰεί κέ σφι φίλη τε καὶ αἰδοίη καλεοίμην.
sentences.tr:
ei keinō epeessi paraipepithousa philon kēr
eis eunēn anesaimi homōthēnai philotēti,
aiei ke sphi philē te kai aidoiē kaleoimēn.
sentences.l:
If those two, with words having won over their dear heart,
I should bring back to the bed, to be united in love,
always dear and revered to them I should be called.”
sentences.i: If I could win those two over with words and bring them back to bed, to be united in love, I should always be called dear and revered by them.”
sentences.n: εἰ … ἀνέσαιμι is a condition with the optative: ‘if I could’. κείνω is the dual accusative ‘those two’. ἐπέεσσι is ‘with words’, and παραιπεπιθοῦσα is the reduplicated aorist participle of παραπείθω ‘win over’, with φίλον κῆρ ‘dear heart’. ἀνέσαιμι, ‘bring back’, is an aorist optative whose verb and exact sense are not certain. ὁμωθῆναι is the aorist passive infinitive ‘to be united’, and φιλότητι ‘in love’. In the main clause κε with the optative καλεοίμην (uncontracted) gives ‘I should be called’, and αἰδοίη ‘revered’ goes with φίλη. This is the end of Hera’s speech.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε φιλομειδὴς Ἀφροδίτη·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ aute proseeipe philomeidēs Aphroditē·
sentences.l: Her then in turn addressed smile-loving Aphrodite:
sentences.i: Then smile-loving Aphrodite spoke to her in turn:
sentences.n: τὴν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε is the reply-formula ‘her then in turn addressed’ (αὖτε marks the second speaker), and φιλομειδής ‘smile-loving’ is Aphrodite’s stock epithet, printed here with a single μ where 5.375 and Odyssey 8.362 print φιλομμειδής. The line is metrically irregular as transmitted: with one μ the short λο of φιλομειδής has to be scanned long, as the first syllable of the fourth foot (the double μ of φιλομμειδής would make it so).

sentences.t: οὐκ ἔστ’ οὐδὲ ἔοικε τεὸν ἔπος ἀρνήσασθαι·
sentences.tr: ouk est’ oude eoike teon epos arnēsasthai·
sentences.l: “It is not possible, nor is it fitting, your word to refuse;
sentences.i: “It is neither possible nor fitting to refuse your word;
sentences.n: οὐκ ἔστ’ is ‘it is not possible’ (ἔστι at the start of the clause means ‘it is possible’), οὐδὲ ἔοικε ‘nor is it fitting’. τεόν is Homeric for σόν ‘your’, and ἔπος ‘word’ is the request. ἀρνήσασθαι is the aorist infinitive of ἀρνέομαι ‘refuse’.

sentences.t: Ζηνὸς γὰρ τοῦ ἀρίστου ἐν ἀγκοίνῃσιν ἰαύεις.
sentences.tr: Zēnos gar tou aristou en ankoinēisin iaueis.
sentences.l: for in the arms of Zeus, the best, you sleep.”
sentences.i: for you sleep in the arms of Zeus, the best.”
sentences.n: Ζηνός is the genitive of Ζεύς, and τοῦ ἀρίστου ‘the best’ uses the article to point him out. ἀγκοίνῃσιν is the epic dative plural, ‘in the arms’, and ἰαύεις ‘you sleep, lie’. γάρ gives Aphrodite’s reason for not refusing: Hera’s place beside Zeus.

sentences.t:
ἦ, καὶ ἀπὸ στήθεσφιν ἐλύσατο κεστὸν ἱμάντα
ποικίλον, ἔνθα δέ οἱ θελκτήρια πάντα τέτυκτο·
sentences.tr:
ē, kai apo stēthesphin elysato keston himanta
poikilon, entha de hoi thelktēria panta tetykto·
sentences.l:
She spoke, and from her breast she loosed the embroidered strap,
intricate, where for her all the charms had been wrought;
sentences.i: So she said, and unfastened from her breast the embroidered strap, intricate, in which all the charms had been wrought;
sentences.n: ἦ, καί is ‘she spoke, and’. ἀπὸ … ἐλύσατο is tmesis, ‘loosed from’ (aorist middle, for herself), and στήθεσφιν has the epic ending -φιν, ‘from her breast’. κεστὸν ἱμάντα is ‘the embroidered strap’: κεστός is traditionally ‘stitched, embroidered’, but its sense is not certain. ποικίλον ‘intricate’, and ἔνθα δέ οἱ θελκτήρια πάντα τέτυκτο is ‘where for her all the charms had been wrought’ (θελκτήριον from θέλγω ‘enchant’; τέτυκτο is the pluperfect passive of τεύχω). The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἔνι μὲν φιλότης, ἐν δ’ ἵμερος, ἐν δ’ ὀαριστὺς
πάρφασις, ἥ τ’ ἔκλεψε νόον πύκα περ φρονεόντων.
sentences.tr:
enth’ eni men philotēs, en d’ himeros, en d’ oaristys
parphasis, hē t’ eklepse noon pyka per phroneontōn.
sentences.l:
There in it was love, and in it longing, and in it intimate talk,
coaxing, which stole the mind even of those thinking shrewdly.
sentences.i: In it were love, longing, and intimate talk, coaxing, which steals the mind even of those who think shrewdly.
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ ἔνι is ‘there in it’. The three items φιλότης ‘love’, ἵμερος ‘longing’ and ὀαριστύς ‘intimate talk’ each have ἐν, and πάρφασις ‘coaxing’ follows with none, in apposition to ὀαριστύς. ἥ is the relative ‘which’, and τε with the aorist ἔκλεψε marks what is always so, ‘steals’. πύκα περ φρονεόντων is ‘even of those thinking shrewdly’ (πύκα ‘closely, shrewdly’).

sentences.t: τόν ῥά οἱ ἔμβαλε χερσὶν ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε·
sentences.tr: ton rha hoi embale chersin epos t’ ephat’ ek t’ onomaze·
sentences.l: This then into her hands she put, and spoke a word and called her by name:
sentences.i: She put it into her hands, and spoke, calling her by name:
sentences.n: τόν is ‘it’, the strap (ἱμάς is masculine), and ῥά ‘then’. οἱ … χερσίν is ‘into her hands’, with οἱ Hera, and ἔμβαλε ‘put in’. ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε is the stock phrase, ‘spoke a word and called by name’ (ἐκ … ὀνόμαζε is tmesis); the speaker is Aphrodite.

sentences.t:
τῆ νῦν τοῦτον ἱμάντα τεῷ ἐγκάτθεο κόλπῳ
ποικίλον, ᾧ ἔνι πάντα τετεύχαται·
sentences.tr:
tē nyn touton himanta teōi enkattheo kolpōi
poikilon, hōi eni panta teteuchatai·
sentences.l:
“Here, now, this strap lay up in your bosom,
intricate, in which all things have been wrought;
sentences.i: “Here, take this intricate strap, in which everything has been wrought, and tuck it into your bosom;
sentences.n: τῆ is ‘here, take this’, with νῦν ‘now’. ἐγκάτθεο is the aorist imperative middle of ἐγκατατίθημι, ‘lay up in’, with τεῷ … κόλπῳ ‘your bosom’ (τεός = σός). ποικίλον agrees with ἱμάντα, and ᾧ ἔνι is ἐν ᾧ ‘in which’. πάντα τετεύχαται is ‘all things have been made’, perfect passive 3rd plural of τεύχω. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 220.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ σέ φημι
ἄπρηκτόν γε νέεσθαι, ὅ τι φρεσὶ σῇσι μενοινᾷς.
sentences.tr:
oude se phēmi
aprēkton ge neesthai, ho ti phresi sēisi menoināis.
sentences.l:
and I tell you, you will not go back fruitless,
whatever in your wits you yearn for.”
sentences.i: and I say you will not go back fruitless, whatever you yearn for in your mind.”
sentences.n: φημί takes the accusative and infinitive: σέ … νέεσθαι is ‘that you will go back’ (νέομαι ‘go, return’, often with a future sense). ἄπρηκτον ‘fruitless’ (ἀ- + πρήσσω ‘accomplish’) agrees with σέ, and γε stresses it. ὅ τι φρεσὶ σῇσι μενοινᾷς is ‘whatever you yearn for in your wits’ (μενοινάω ‘yearn’; σῇσι is ‘your’). This is the end of Aphrodite’s speech.
